statement: After H4's sea trials, the Board commissioned Kendall to copy it; K1's 1769 completion and Cook-voyage operation provide a named replication by another maker, not evidence of economical serial manufacture.

sources.supports: 1766 commission, 1769 completion and second Cook voyage use.
Contemporary account presents the commission as a test of another maker's execution.

counterevidence: The obituary's approximate delivery date differs; RMG's completion date is used, with the disagreement preserved.
inference_limits: One copy establishes neither typical manufacturing yield nor fleet-wide access.

test.reason: Identifies a particular copy and trial, without assigning a causal effect to commission funding.

statement: Kendall's obituary reports cleaning K1 in 1775 and, after deterioration and stoppage on Cook's third voyage, replacing some corroded parts; a working precision artifact therefore did not remove the need for service during its useful life.

sources.supports: Reports disassembly/cleaning, altered rate, stoppage and rust requiring new parts.

counterevidence: The account is laudatory and cannot establish whether contamination, handling, design or another cause produced the failure.
inference_limits: No breakdown probability or comparative maintenance cost is inferred.

test.mechanism_chain: Long voyage exposure/operation -> rate change and deterioration -> service and part replacement -> repair work on a still-valued instrument.
test.strongest_rival: Exceptional mistreatment, not an inherent design burden, may explain this breakdown.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable watches with documented handling/cleaning and rate histories would separate design vulnerability from an exceptional service episode.
test.evidence_sought_found: S02 explicitly records both successful voyages and later corrosion; no matched watch/handling records inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Shows actual maintenance work, but not why that amount was needed or how representative it was.

statement: In the late eighteenth-century navigation system described by Higgitt, marine timekeepers and astronomical observations were used together; chronometer deployment did not make local-time observation or independent checks dispensable.

sources.locator: Investing in longitude and Navigation systems, notes 24 and 28–33
sources.supports: Joint trials, local time comparison, calibration and continued astronomical practice.

counterevidence: Relative reliance on methods differed by voyage and task; ordinary dead reckoning persisted.
inference_limits: No claim that every navigator made every observation or that one method was always best.

test.mechanism_chain: Portable reference time + observed local time/rate checks -> usable longitude comparison -> complementary instrument/observer work.
test.strongest_rival: A simple replacement account predicts astronomy becomes unnecessary when a good watch arrives.
test.discriminating_observation: Named joint use and the need to identify/restore a disturbed reference would contradict complete replacement.
test.evidence_sought_found: S03 describes combined Cook trials, calibration and local-time measurements; mathematical comparison also requires both reference and local information.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Chronometer convenience may reduce some lunar work; complementarity does not imply equal effort or unchanged practice.

statement: Japanese clockmakers served seasonal-hour conventions through different mechanisms, including alternating foliots and movable hour markers; many required periodic human adjustment rather than adoption of equal-hour time.

sources.supports: Explains alternating foliots, marker adjustment and two automatic exceptions.
Defines seasonal-hour system and recurring adjustment.

counterevidence: Surviving examples overrepresent durable/collectable artifacts; local calendars and practice were not necessarily uniform.
inference_limits: Technical alternatives do not establish nationwide household ownership or punctuality.

test.reason: Describes documented mechanism configurations and operator tasks, not the cause or prevalence of their adoption.

statement: Tanaka's 1851 Myriad Year Clock automated seasonal markers, yet Hashimoto reports only one completed clock and no buyer despite an intention to sell more; exceptional mechanical elaboration did not itself establish a scalable product.

sources.supports: Disassembly account, complex mechanism and unsold single-clock history; price-refusal story is explicitly anecdotal.

counterevidence: Tanaka subsequently changed work under patronage; opportunity costs and lack of marketing may rival price/complexity. The purchaser story is not an account ledger.
inference_limits: No calculated profitability, buyer willingness-to-pay or typical Japanese manufacturing limit.

test.mechanism_chain: Elaborate automatically adjusting design -> costly/complex individual artifact -> intended elite sale fails -> no observed repeated production.
test.strongest_rival: A career change or limited sales opportunity, rather than excessive complexity, explains the singular output.
test.discriminating_observation: Workshop accounts, offers, orders and later reproduction attempts could distinguish price/production constraints from changed priorities.
test.evidence_sought_found: S04 supplies artifact study and biographical sales narrative, but not accounts or a reproducibility trial by another maker.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Single output is better established than its cause; complexity is not treated as a sufficient explanation.

statement: Tanaka's documented career combined commercial craft work, instruction in calendrical theory/practice from the Tsuchimikado family in 1847, and later Saga patronage; the exact tools used to make his clock's fine components remain uncertain.

sources.supports: Shop/patronage sequence, specialist instruction and explicit uncertainty about clockmaking tools.

counterevidence: Career reconstruction relies partly on biographies and selected surviving records; some youthful-inventor anecdotes are unreliable.
inference_limits: This is a named route to expertise, not proof of the necessary educational sequence or relative contributions of teaching and self-practice.

test.reason: Records known learning/work settings and a material knowledge gap; makes no necessity claim for tacit transmission.

statement: Hall's 1811 rifle patent preceded his 1819 government contract and years of tooling; his and Talcott's statements describe reduced dependence on handwork, not the elimination of skilled toolmaking or measured gains for workers.

sources.supports: Separates patent, procurement, tooling and contemporaries' assertions about ordinary labour/machinery.
Main factory's piece-rate and 55-task organisation already existed by 1816.

counterevidence: Hall was defending his project, and the museum page is celebratory; no independent cost or skill inventory is provided.
inference_limits: Cannot infer net deskilling, lower full cost or higher wages from promoters' statements.

test.reason: Sequences institutional events and identifies the limits of contemporary labour assertions.

statement: The Harpers Ferry standardisation account describes working gauges checked against a separate gauge set, so repeated dimensions were supported by maintained measurement references as well as machines; the later HAFE7427 set documents physical inspection equipment.

sources.supports: 1823 gauge adoption and separate gauges to check working gauges.
Surviving Model 1841 inspection set attributed to Thornton; same set as S06 figure 19.

counterevidence: A gauge can wear or be used incorrectly; its existence alone does not show output conformed. Different model and workshop dates cannot be combined into one universal system.
inference_limits: No tolerance values, rejection rates or universal necessity of this exact gauge system are claimed.

test.mechanism_chain: Component variation -> comparison with gauges -> checking working gauges against references -> a repeatable basis for accepting dimensions.
test.strongest_rival: Machines alone deliver sufficient repeatability, with inspection merely ceremonial.
test.discriminating_observation: Documented checks on the gauges themselves are more expected when measurement drift matters than when machine output is self-validating.
test.evidence_sought_found: S06 explicitly describes reference checking; S12 supplies a later physical set but no actual pass/fail dataset.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Operational importance is supported; marginal effects on yield/cost remain unidentified.

statement: A1829 examination of Harpers Ferry Model 1816 muskets made in 1819–1820 still found incomplete interchangeability, according to the NPS report's Schmidt-based account; Hall's rifle-work claims cannot be applied to every armory model.

sources.supports: Identifies inspected model/production dates and reports good overall quality with defects and incomplete interchangeability.

counterevidence: The original inspection report was not acquired; the report does not supply a component pass-rate denominator here.
inference_limits: Different product designs and factories prevent this from being a matched causal comparison.

test.reason: A bounded negative observation that limits the population to which a success claim can apply.

statement: In Grace's garage evidence, novices moved through supervised routine maintenance, physical assistance and more specialised repair; apprenticeship exchanged labour for instruction and small shares of profits, and included cleaning/cooking or errands alongside mechanical tasks.

sources.supports: Direct observation and oral histories of allocation of tasks, supervision, support and gradual access to specialised work.

counterevidence: Interview narratives stress intelligence and omit routine work; author participation helps reveal this but was short and not representative.
inference_limits: No typical learning duration, graduation probability or monetary return is established.

test.reason: Describes witnessed and reported training practices, distinguishing later observation from historical recollection.

statement: Personal tool accumulation could widen apprentices' ability to take work outside a garage; Grace records salvaged tools and one mechanic's growth from an under-tree shop in 1967 to larger premises and welding equipment in 1972.

sources.supports: Links own wrenches/tools to independent work and provides Juma Katigiro's dated account.

counterevidence: Customer connections, skill and demand grow together with tools; failed entrants are poorly observed.
inference_limits: One career and qualitative accounts do not identify an asset effect or prove tools alone suffice.

test.mechanism_chain: Participation -> accumulation of usable tools and skill -> ability to accept some independent jobs -> possible workshop autonomy.
test.strongest_rival: Demand/reputation alone drives both tool purchases and independent work; tools may proxy success.
test.discriminating_observation: Track otherwise comparable apprentices before and after obtaining tools, including those who never exit and job types needing particular equipment.
test.evidence_sought_found: S08 links particular tools to tasks and narrates one expansion, but gives no apprentice cohort or exogenous tool access.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Tools have a concrete task role; their marginal contribution to entry or income remains unknown.

statement: Grace records both hand-based and machine-assisted automotive repair, and disputes over their reliability; some mechanics preferred stock modules, manuals or model specialisation over extensive improvisation.

sources.supports: Regional machine access, hand refinishing, contested quality, modular reliability, manuals and specialisation.

counterevidence: Mechanics' reputational criticism may be self-serving; observed continued use does not establish comparative safety or long life.
inference_limits: Repair-based alternatives are real, but their desirability cannot be ranked without costs, workloads, durability and user risks.

test.mechanism_chain: Changing parts/machine access -> choice among manual fabrication, reuse or stock-module repair -> continued service with variable effort/reliability.
test.strongest_rival: Regional mechanical cultures or reputation strategies, rather than access alone, explain method differences.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare like repairs with measured equipment/parts availability, labour time and subsequent failure under similar loads.
test.evidence_sought_found: S08 describes alternative methods and explicit disagreement, including preference for original modules; no comparative lifetime tests found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Access, skill, culture and vehicle mix vary jointly; no universal superiority of either ingenuity or standard replacement.

statement: Most technicians in Mchome's interview sample said they had formal vocational training and also acquired experience through informal practice after graduation; the evidence does not support an exclusive formal-versus-informal skills dichotomy.

sources.supports: Interview method and technicians' reports of combined learning routes.

counterevidence: Educational statistics are expressly unavailable; formal-training claims are self-reported and the sample is nonrepresentative.
inference_limits: No estimate of the added value of either training route or national technician composition.

test.reason: Reports a defined interview finding and its sample limit, not an effect of training on repair performance.

statement: Dar es Salaam users in Mchome's study reported continuing to use repaired appliances, including one television four years after repair; component repair offered a route to retained service alongside replacement or going without.

sources.supports: Customer report of television repair and continued use; description of power-supply/component work.

counterevidence: Failed repairs, safety problems and dissatisfied customers may be underrepresented; technician explanations of voltage incompatibility were not independently tested.
inference_limits: No citywide resilience effect, failure rate or engineering approval of the modifications is implied.

test.mechanism_chain: Damaged appliance + constrained replacement budget -> paid repair/component work -> reported restored and continued service.
test.strongest_rival: Only easily repaired devices/successful customers entered the interview record; durable outcomes reflect selection rather than general repair effectiveness.
test.discriminating_observation: Follow all attempted repairs, including failures, and compare service life/cost/safety with matched replacements and unrepaired devices.
test.evidence_sought_found: S09 includes a concrete four-year user report and descriptions of interventions, but lacks a repair cohort or controlled tests.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The existence of a successful route is supported; its frequency, comparative durability and net welfare effect remain unresolved.

statement: Mchome proposes that1990s utility retrenchment helped move trained personnel into street electrical work, but the inspected account cannot separate computerisation/prepaid metering from simultaneous structural-adjustment job cuts or measure workers' subsequent livelihoods.

sources.supports: Tanesco training history, restructuring, retirement/freelance pathway and temporary-work networks.

counterevidence: Much of the account inherits other studies; no matched staff cohorts or complete employment sequence is provided.
inference_limits: A plausible occupational transition is not evidence that technology alone caused job loss or that informal work compensated for it.

test.mechanism_chain: Utility reorganisation/technology/policy change -> lower-tier workforce reduction -> some trained workers sell outside services -> enlarged informal labour supply.
test.strongest_rival: Fiscal retrenchment independently causes job loss, while rising appliance imports/demand independently attracts freelancers.
test.discriminating_observation: Personnel records linking tasks, dismissal dates, technology rollout and post-exit earnings could distinguish the pathways.
test.evidence_sought_found: S09 describes all these coincident changes and links some retired workers to freelance work; such personnel/earnings data were not inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Supply and demand changes, causal order and magnitude remain unresolved.

statement: Among the early TEA-laser laboratories Collins investigated, written-only attempts had not succeeded and working copies were associated with contact with successful builders; visits sometimes failed, and the author explicitly did not claim written-only success was impossible.

sources.supports: Network scope/search checks, successes/failures, contact routes and explicit generalisation caveat.

counterevidence: Contact is selected, not random; early papers often omitted details deliberately, and unseen isolated successes might remain.
inference_limits: Supports a bounded role for contact, not an indispensable invisible ingredient in every technology or permanent impossibility of codification.

test.mechanism_chain: Early incomplete instructions + uncertain implementation -> visits/calls/placements -> additional practical information/experience -> working copies in observed network.
test.strongest_rival: Successful labs have greater prior expertise/resources, or merely receive missing explicit details; either can produce the same contact-success association.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable labs assigned complete validated instructions, components and contact conditions, or documented later successful independent builds, would discriminate stronger tacit necessity.
test.evidence_sought_found: S10 searched for isolates through three supplementary routes and reports no written-only successes, but also failed contacts and improving instructions in p. 176 note 26.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Contact packages expertise, disclosure, material advice and selection; these are not separately identified.

statement: For some double-discharge TEA builds, demanding electrode-profile tolerances obstructed one laboratory while roughly filed profiles and aluminium banister rail worked elsewhere; the episode limits a general 'more precision solves replication' explanation.

sources.supports: Contrasts insuperable machining requirements with two reported successful rougher alternatives.

counterevidence: Other circuit and geometry differences may explain cross-laboratory outcomes; not all TEA designs share one tolerance envelope.
inference_limits: No numerical engineering tolerance or claim that precision is useless; these are historical observations, not construction instructions.

test.mechanism_chain: Uncertain design significance -> overly strict interpreted machining demand -> blocked build; alternative builders use looser geometry -> operation in those configurations.
test.strongest_rival: Strict geometry is necessary in the blocked lab's other configuration, while alternative circuitry permits rougher parts.
test.discriminating_observation: Hold the rest of the configuration fixed while varying verified electrode geometry and measuring output/reliability.
test.evidence_sought_found: S10 reports the striking contrast but no controlled common-configuration test.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The reported rougher alternatives reject a categorical all-configurations strict-precision requirement. They do not distinguish the named configuration-specific rival; no controlled common-configuration substitution or reliability comparison is reported.

statement: Accessible footnotes to Collins and Harrison's1975 follow-up record simultaneous changes to two build variables and repeated power-unit failures; those observations leave any exclusive knowledge-transfer explanation of that episode's delays underdetermined.

sources.supports: Two variables changed together; teaching burden; at least six power-unit failures byJune1975; available written advice was not always consulted.

counterevidence: Full narrative was not acquired, so the total chronology or authors' full causal explanation is not reconstructed.
inference_limits: Hardware reliability and time allocation are demonstrated candidate confounders, not measured shares of delay.

test.mechanism_chain: Build difficulties -> simultaneous adjustments and repairs amid time constraints -> eventual observations cannot isolate each input's effect.
test.strongest_rival: Learning alone explains progress; hardware failures are consequences of inexperienced construction rather than independent causes.
test.discriminating_observation: Contemporaneous logs and one-variable interventions distinguishing component faults, operator experience and available time.
test.evidence_sought_found: S11 footnotes explicitly state the simultaneous changes, teaching load and repeated failures; no complete log/body text inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Reciprocal causation between learning and hardware failures remains possible.
